newsitem.title: USA: Too little time to make CRP rule work - US skeptics.
newsitem.headline: Too little time to make CRP rule work - US skeptics.

text.p: The Agriculture Department may be overloading itself by promising to enroll up to 22 million acres of land in the Conservation Reserve by early summer, U.S. lawmakers and farm groups said Wednesday.
Sign-up for the revamped reserve will open Monday and close March 28. Tens of thousands of farmers could submit bids. Each would be assessed on a 26-page form.

Acting Undersecretary Dallas Smith said the decision on which land to accept would be made by early June. Members of a House Agriculture subcommittee were skeptical and noted the department was woefully late in drafting new operating rules for the program.

Some farm groups also were wary. The National Association of Wheat Growers said it feared the new rules would be biased against wheat acreage by offering too low a rental rate. NAWG and the National Cotton Council urged a one-year extension of expiring Conservation Reserve contracts.
"The best thing we could do is extend the current contracts for a year so we don't jump off a cliff," said Representative Colin Peterson, Minnesota Democrat.

Created in 1985, the reserve pays farmers an annual rent in exchange for idling fragile land for 10 years. Average cost is $1.9 billion a year. Congress reauthorized the reserve last year and refocused its goals slightly.
Contracts on about 22 million acres were due to expire this fall, setting the stage for a huge turn-over in the reserve, which can hold up to 36.4 million acres.
Smith and three aides repeatedly assured the subcommittee the switch-over would proceed smoothly.

The American Farmland Trust, a conservation group, suggested a gradual start to the chore. Some eight million to 10 million acres could be enrolled this spring, it said, with more land to be enrolled after a new round of bids later in the year.

Representative Cal Dooley, California Democrat, urged the department to keep its eye on the reserves's goal -- less soil erosion, protection of water quality and more wildlife habitat -- rather than focusing on maximum acreage enrollment.
The American Farm Bureau Federation said it worried there would be delays while federal workers learned how to use the "environmental benefits index" that ranks land.
The Coalition for a Competitive Food and Agricultura System, a coalition of agribusiness groups, counseled a prudent review to make sure productive land returned to crop use.
"In order to enroll land with the most environmental benefit, USDA may need to conduct several signups," the coalition said.
